patient.name: Lena Marchetti
patient.chief_complaint: Two years of asymmetric leg pain and weakness, worse on the left, with recent right foot drop
patient.hpi: Lena Marchetti is a 51-year-old schoolteacher presenting with a 2-year history of progressive and strikingly asymmetric lower extremity symptoms. The illness began with severe burning pain in her left calf and thigh, initially attributed to lumbar radiculopathy by her primary care physician. An MRI lumbar spine 18 months ago showed moderate L3-L4 and L4-L5 stenosis, and she underwent two epidural steroid injections without sustained benefit. Over the subsequent year, she developed right foot drop with steppage gait on the right, which was abrupt in onset over 3 days. Her left leg pain persists but has partly improved. She also notes intermittent right hand clumsiness and occasional elbow area pain on the right. There is no classic glove-and-stocking numbness. She denies bowel or bladder dysfunction. Her diabetes was diagnosed 6 months ago during workup for this presentation — HbA1c was 6.9%. She has lost 8 kg over the past year without trying, which she initially attributed to reduced appetite from pain. She denies fever, rash, oral ulcers, or joint swelling. Past medical history includes a remote episode of pleuritis 8 years ago, attributed to 'viral illness' at the time but never formally evaluated. She takes no immunosuppressants. Her symptoms and the asymmetric stepwise pattern have been puzzling to her treating physicians.
pmh: Type 2 diabetes (newly diagnosed 6 months ago, HbA1c 6.9%)
Lumbar spondylosis with L3-L4 and L4-L5 stenosis (prior epidural steroid injections x2)
Remote pleuritis 8 years ago (not fully evaluated)

Gabapentin 300 mg three times daily (neuropathic pain — partially effective)

report.summary: ASYMMETRIC MULTIFOCAL NEUROPATHY consistent with mononeuritis multiplex. Acute right peroneal neuropathy (right foot drop). Subacute axonal pattern in left leg. Mild right ulnar neuropathy. Pattern is NOT consistent with typical diabetic length-dependent neuropathy nor CIDP. Vasculitic neuropathy must be excluded.

motor.flag: SEVERELY REDUCED AMPLITUDE — acute axonal loss right peroneal
motor.note: Fibular head stimulation: amplitude 0.3 mV — no conduction block; axonal degeneration

sensory.flag: severely reduced — right sural axonal loss
severely reduced — right peroneal sensory axonal loss

muscles_tested.recruitment: severely reduced — few MUPs firing rapidly
muscles_tested.morphology: normal morphology (insufficient time for reinnervation — acute lesion)

emg.summary: Acute severe denervation in right peroneal territory (3+ fibrillations) contrasting with chronic changes in left leg and right ulnar territory — MONONEURITIS MULTIPLEX pattern. This is NOT diabetic polyneuropathy.

report.overall_impression: MONONEURITIS MULTIPLEX. Stepwise asymmetric involvement of right peroneal (acute), left tibial/peroneal (subacute), and right ulnar (mild). Amplitude-predominant loss consistent with axonal degeneration rather than demyelination. DIFFERENTIAL: vasculitic neuropathy (Sjögren's, SLE, ANCA-associated), non-vasculitic Sjögren's neuropathy (sensory ataxic or ganglionopathy), diabetic amyotrophy/lumbosacral radiculoplexopathy. URGENT: nerve biopsy to exclude vasculitis.

report.summary: VASCULITIC NEUROPATHY. Epineurial vessel wall inflammation with transmural neutrophilic infiltrate and fibrinoid necrosis. Axonal degeneration in multiple fascicles. Findings confirm epineurial vasculitis consistent with Sjögren's syndrome-associated vasculitic neuropathy.
report.histology: Multiple sections of right sural nerve examined. Epineurial arteriole: transmural inflammation with neutrophilic and lymphocytic infiltrate, fibrinoid necrosis of vessel wall, obliteration of vascular lumen. Perivascular CD3+ T lymphocytes and CD20+ B lymphocytes. Multiple fascicles show axonal degeneration (reduced myelinated fiber density, Wallerian degeneration). No granulomas. CD31 staining confirms vascular involvement. Congo red negative.
report.interpretation: EPINEURIAL VASCULITIS — vasculitic neuropathy confirmed. In the clinical context of anti-SSA/SSB positivity, pattern consistent with Sjögren's syndrome-associated vasculitic neuropathy. Treatment: high-dose corticosteroids + immunosuppression (cyclophosphamide or azathioprine). Rheumatology co-management essential.

report.summary: Minor salivary gland biopsy: focus score 2 foci/4 mm². Lymphocytic sialadenitis confirmed. Findings consistent with primary Sjögren's syndrome.
report.histology: Six minor salivary gland lobules examined. Periductal lymphocytic infiltrates forming 2 distinct foci per 4 mm² (focus score ≥1 is diagnostic threshold for Sjögren's). Lymphocytes predominantly CD4+ T cells with scattered B cells. Acinar atrophy in affected lobules. No granulomas.
report.interpretation: POSITIVE LIP BIOPSY — focus score 2/4 mm². Combined with anti-SSA >240 U/mL and clinical features, meets 2016 ACR/EULAR criteria for primary Sjögren's syndrome (score ≥4). Vasculitic neuropathy is an extraglandular manifestation of Sjögren's.

report.summary: AUTONOMIC TESTING: Mildly abnormal sympathetic sudomotor function on QSART (reduced sweat output bilateral feet and legs). Heart rate variability reduced at rest. Findings consistent with mild autonomic involvement in the context of vasculitic neuropathy. No orthostatic hypotension on tilt table testing. Autonomic involvement in Sjögren's neuropathy can include sudomotor dysfunction.

critical_actions: Recognize mononeuritis multiplex pattern on NCS/EMG — do NOT attribute to diabetic polyneuropathy
Order anti-SSA/SSB given systemic features (weight loss, prior pleuritis, anemia with eosinophilia)
Sural nerve biopsy to confirm vasculitic neuropathy before long-term immunosuppression
High-dose steroids for active vasculitic neuropathy — nerve damage is irreversible without treatment
Urinalysis with microscopy + 24-hour protein — exclude nephritis
contraindicated_actions: Do not attribute right foot drop to lumbar radiculopathy without nerve biopsy — NCS pattern argues against root-level lesion
Do not continue only symptomatic gabapentin — vasculitic neuropathy requires immunosuppression
Do not start IVIG for CIDP — this is vasculitic neuropathy requiring steroids + immunosuppression, not CIDP
Do not delay nerve biopsy while awaiting all autoimmune results — severity of foot drop requires urgent treatment decision

differential.key_distinguishing: HbA1c 6.9% (early diabetes); diabetic neuropathy is length-dependent symmetric axonal polyneuropathy — not mononeuritis multiplex with right foot drop and left thigh pain
Moderate stenosis on MRI does not account for 2/5 foot drop or multifocal pattern; NCS shows multifocal axonal loss not root-level abnormality; epidural injections failed
Anti-dsDNA only borderline, renal biopsy TIN (not lupus nephritis pattern), lip biopsy confirms Sjögren's as primary diagnosis; SLE overlap cannot be fully excluded but insufficient criteria
ANCA (MPO/PR3) negative; nerve biopsy pattern more consistent with immune complex vasculitis than ANCA-associated small vessel vasculitis

key_reasoning_points: MODERATE DIFFICULTY: The new diabetes diagnosis and prior lumbar spine imaging create powerful anchoring bias toward diabetic radiculopathy/neuropathy
KEY DISCRIMINATOR: Asymmetric abrupt right foot drop with acute denervation (3+ fibrillations) on EMG — classic mononeuritis multiplex, not diabetic pattern
Sjögren's syndrome is significantly under-recognized as cause of neuropathy; anti-SSA/SSB should be tested in any asymmetric or unusual neuropathy
Lumbar stenosis is a common red herring — epidural injections temporarily masking inflammatory pain explains partial response
Weight loss + prior pleuritis + anemia + mild eosinophilia are systemic clues pointing away from pure metabolic neuropathy
Nerve biopsy is essential — vasculitic neuropathy requires histologic confirmation before cytotoxic therapy
Low complement (C3/C4) in Sjögren's indicates systemic immune complex disease and correlates with vasculitis risk
